questions.q: What does the X gate do to the state |0⟩?
questions.explain: X = [[0,1],[1,0]]. Multiplying by the column vector [1,0]ᵀ for |0⟩ gives [0,1]ᵀ, which is |1⟩ with no phase factor attached. X is a pure bit flip — the 'quantum NOT' — with none of the phase behavior that Y introduces.

questions.q: Direct matrix-vector computation shows Y|0⟩ equals which state?
questions.explain: Representing i as the pair [0,1] and multiplying Y=[[0,-i],[i,0]] by [1,0]ᵀ gives amplitude 0 on |0⟩ and amplitude i on |1⟩, i.e. Y|0⟩ = i|1⟩. Y bundles the same bit flip X performs with an extra ±i phase factor, with the sign depending on the direction of the flip.

questions.q: Applying Z to the state (1/√2)|0⟩ + (1/√2)|1⟩ produces (1/√2)|0⟩ − (1/√2)|1⟩. What happens to the measurement probabilities for outcomes 0 and 1?
questions.explain: Squaring the magnitude of each amplitude before Z gives |1/√2|²=0.5 for each outcome, and after Z the amplitudes are 1/√2 and −1/√2, whose squared magnitudes are still 0.5 and 0.5. Measurement only depends on |amplitude|², and squaring erases the minus sign, so a sign-only change (relative phase) is invisible to a direct measurement in this basis.

questions.q: Which Pauli gate leaves |0⟩ completely unchanged while only altering the sign of |1⟩'s amplitude?
questions.explain: Z = [[1,0],[0,-1]]. Multiplying by |0⟩ = [1,0]ᵀ returns [1,0]ᵀ exactly (unchanged), while multiplying by |1⟩ = [0,1]ᵀ returns [0,-1]ᵀ, i.e. -|1⟩. X and Y both change which basis state the amplitude sits on (a genuine bit flip); Z never does — it is a pure phase flip.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize that Z's effect is 'invisible' to a direct measurement, but still matters for later algorithms?
options: Because Z is not actually a valid unitary gate

Because a relative phase like the sign flip from Z has no effect on |amplitude|² by itself, but becomes observable once combined with a gate like Hadamard that converts phase differences into amplitude differences
Because Z only works on multi-qubit states, not single qubits
Because Z changes the normalization of the state vector
questions.explain: A relative phase (here, a sign) squares away under |amplitude|² and so cannot be detected by measuring the qubit alone in the computational basis. But phase is real information stored in the state vector, and gates such as Hadamard (next lesson) can turn that phase difference into a measurable amplitude difference — this is the foundation of interference-based quantum algorithms.
